paragraphs.heading: A hollow left by collapse
paragraphs.text: A caldera is a large hollow shaped like a cauldron. It forms shortly after a volcanic eruption empties a magma chamber. The word is Spanish and goes back to the Latin caldaria, which means "cooking pot". A caldera is sometimes described as a crater, but it is really a kind of sinkhole, since it forms by sinking and collapse and not by an explosion or impact.

paragraphs.heading: How the ground gives way
paragraphs.text: Throwing out a large volume of magma in a short time removes much of what filled the chamber. Its walls and ceiling may then be unable to carry their own weight and the rock resting above. A roughly circular fracture, called the ring fault, develops around the chamber's edge. As the chamber empties, the centre of the volcano inside that ring begins to collapse. This may happen in a single cataclysmic eruption or in stages over a series of eruptions. The total area that drops may be hundreds of square kilometres.

paragraphs.heading: A rare event
paragraphs.text: Thousands of volcanic eruptions take place over a century, but a caldera forms only a few times in any given 100 years. Only nine caldera-forming collapses are known between 1911 and 2022. The most recent were at Kīlauea in Hawaii in 2018 and at Hunga Tonga–Hunga Haʻapai in 2022.

paragraphs.heading: Different kinds of trigger
paragraphs.text: What sets off a collapse is the magma chamber under the volcano being emptied. Sometimes a large explosive eruption does this, as at Tambora in 1815. It can also happen during effusive eruptions on a volcano's flanks, as at Piton de la Fournaise in 2007. A third route is an effusive eruption in a connected fissure system, as at Bárðarbunga in 2014–2015.

paragraphs.heading: Inside an explosive eruption
paragraphs.text: Explosive caldera eruptions come from chambers whose magma is rich in silica. Such magma has a high viscosity, so it does not flow easily the way basalt does. It typically also holds a large amount of dissolved gas. Near the surface the pressure on the magma drops, and the trapped gas bubbles out rapidly, breaking the magma into volcanic ash and other tephra mixed with very hot gas. This mixture first rises into the atmosphere as an eruption column. As more material erupts, the column cannot take in enough air to stay buoyant, so it collapses and falls back to the surface as pyroclastic flows.

paragraphs.heading: The scale of the largest
paragraphs.text: In a single event, a silicic caldera may erupt hundreds of cubic kilometres of material, or even thousands. Yellowstone Caldera last erupted some 650,000 years ago. That eruption released about 1,000 km³ of material, and debris up to two metres deep covered a substantial part of North America. Eruptions forming even larger calderas are known. At La Garita Caldera in Colorado, the 5,000 cubic kilometre Fish Canyon Tuff was blasted out about 27.8 million years ago. Even a small caldera-forming eruption, like Krakatoa in 1883 or Mount Pinatubo in 1991, may bring significant destruction locally and a noticeable drop in temperature worldwide.

paragraphs.heading: What happens afterwards
paragraphs.text: After eruptions like these, the caldera typically fills in with tuff, rhyolite and other igneous rocks. If magma keeps being injected into the collapsed chamber, the centre of the caldera may be lifted into what is called a resurgent dome, as seen at Yellowstone and Lake Toba. Some calderas are also known to hold rich ore deposits. Metal-rich fluids can circulate through a caldera and form ore deposits of metals, among them lead, silver, gold, mercury, lithium and uranium.
